Constitutional Law is the body of legal principles governing how governments function, the rights of citizens, and the distribution of power among branches and levels of authority. Rooted in the Magna Carta's assertion that even kings are bound by law, constitutional law developed as a discipline reconciling popular sovereignty with governmental stability. In democracies, courts interpret constitutions to resolve conflicts between branches, protect individual rights, and adapt foundational documents to changing times. The Magna Carta, issued in 1215, established the principle that governmental authority is limited by law and subject to legal constraints—a foundational idea for all subsequent constitutional thinking. Written constitutions, like the United States Constitution of 1787, attempted to codify governmental structure and individual rights in a permanent, supreme law amendable only through extraordinary process. Constitutional interpretation involves courts deciding what constitutional provisions mean when applied to novel circumstances. This interpretive authority makes courts powerful arbiters of governmental legitimacy. The doctrine of judicial review, firmly established in Marbury v. Madison in 1803, empowered courts to strike down unconstitutional laws and governmental actions conflicting with constitutional provisions. Major constitutional struggles center on federalism—central versus state power—separation of powers among executive, legislative, and judicial branches, and individual rights including liberty, equality, and due process. Landmark constitutional cases like Brown v. Board of Education and Loving v. Virginia expanded fundamental rights protections through judicial interpretation rather than requiring textual constitutional amendments. Constitutional amendments, like the Fourteenth Amendment, have explicitly expanded rights and constrained governmental power, reflecting political will to revise foundational law. Constitutional jurisprudence varies significantly by country. Britain relies on parliamentary sovereignty and convention. Germany emphasizes human dignity. India balances federalism with rights. The United States emphasizes judicial review and protection of individual rights.
